new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive; by default it falls on the word-initial syllable ('the most dominant tendency'). Deviations are conditioned by syllable content and morphology: a tri-consonantal cluster draws the stress peak onto its first (sonorant) member (e.g. /jajnja-n/ [dzaíndzan], /gulgura-j-n-gan/ [gołgoraíngan]), a long [i:] outranks such a cluster, and certain suffixes (e.g. -bara 'denizen', -gali-) shift stress to the following vowel (jámba vs jambábara, bálgan vs balgágalen), while others do not (gámo, gámonga). Because placement depends on clusters/length and on particular suffixes rather than on syllable count alone, read as default-initial but weight/morphology-sensitive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress appears in the snippets obtained; unknown whether sec. 2.7 discusses it (pp. 133 and 141 not re-fetched sources).
new_statements.exceptions: p.136: 'there are exceptions, in which stress does not fall on initial phoneme of a tri-consonantal cluster. The reason for this is not known' (e.g. /bujnjul/ [boindʒól]-type forms); suffix-induced stress shift applies to 'certain (though not all) suffixes' and 'the data are far from complete, and details are not known' (p.136); earlier in-house reader also noted p.141 words with non-initial stress such as /gandaru/. p.133 (per earlier reader and Davis 2012 notice): stress 'is not distinctive... Nonetheless, it does exist phonetically.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms of roots and suffixed words from a single main speaker, Alf Palmer); pitch treated separately (p.141, 'not distinctive' per Davis 2012). Access caveat: text read only as ~300-character verbatim Google Books snippets with page numbers, saved as JSON; the full pages 133-141 were not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Tsunoda 2011 describes Warrongo (waru1264) almost entirely from one speaker, Alf Palmer (Jinbilnggay), recorded 1971-74 on the upper Herbert River; the two 1970s speakers probably represented different dialects (Davis 2012 notice, citing p. 3-4). Not to be confused with neighbouring Warrgamay (warr1255, Dixon HAL vol. 2) or Gugu-Badhun (gugu1253, Sutton 1973). WALS code wgu; no StressTyp2/WALS stress entry exists.
